title: The Works of Christ and the Spirit in Creation
english: He strove against their incurable diseases; after all those things the Savior came appropriately, healing every disease and every weakness, even to raise up their corruption and death. For this reason the Savior shone forth the truth in the times of Augustus, when the time was fulfilled so that the things of human salvation happened accordingly.

Concerning this the present word says: 'It is a time to have mercy on Zion, O Lord, and You, rising on Your own, will have mercy on her' (Ps 102). Thanksgiving was necessary to follow the preceding prophecy. This too is arranged through this song: the mercy of God and the critical justice are glorified, that through mercy He will rescue the people from the wrongdoers; the removal of corruption, and the grace preserved for successors, and the kingdom of heaven that will pass over all things.

It is not that the heaven surrounds the whole thing and covers it, but it roofs the earth spread out around it, being covered from above by waters in a permanent and firm standing (Ps 103). It is evident, then, that the 'Extending' and 'Roofing' and 'Making' is instead the 'one who extended' and 'one who roofed' and 'one who made.' So it is also with the 'Forming' spirit of man within him; the forming having occurred by God once for the earth, and the results from it happen forever, just as it is said, 'My Father is working until now, and I am working' (John 5:17). And 'I am the Being' would also contribute to this, as the works are not non-existent but are becoming, having the nature of the becoming, and therefore their being is understood in the becoming and is not actually existing like the maker. This is permeated through the Holy Trinity being creative.

Regarding the wonderful thing, it says of the founding of God's power: the earth, being the heaviest element, having been set beneath the waters and remaining immovable for an age, is not perhaps supported by the abyss that lies beneath, nor is it settling, but is covering [the abyss] in the manner of garments, so that the seat may be unutterable and of God's power, not of the nature of elements (Ps 103). The earth gives these things, springs of water gushing from the beginning by the power of God (Ps 103), and says that many things are driven into disappearance by the fear of God, which is stated more clearly in the seventy-third [Psalm]: 'You burst the springs and...'

Rivers, you dried up other rivers. He marvels also at the position of the mountains, having been raised unchangeably over the plains and not being dragged down by the descending mist to cover the underlying things, according to the Erusi: 'Cover us, O mountains' (Ps 103:13).

He calls the air of the high heavens the work of God, just as it is over one house of the whole world. And he calls the rain the work of the Son, from which the earth bears fruit in abundance (Ps 103:17). And he calls the lifting up of the waters from the sea the work [of the Son] (Ps 103:17b).

And concerning the wild donkey it is said through Jeremiah: 'Even the wild donkey in the heavens has known its times' (Ps 103:26b). And regarding his calming, it is said that God [calms him], that is, to set his cunning to nothing. For God laughs at everything that opposes him, because it is placed in vanity and childishness because it is easily burned, just as it is said concerning the Egyptians: 'How many follies I have performed against the Egyptians' (Ps 103:27-28).

[Others will take the provided text regarding the food provided to the animals. For when this is present, it is abundant and rejoices; but when it is absent, it is pressed and poured out by the lack of necessities (Ps 103:29-30).]

This is the work of Christ, who also says that resurrection is to be, and life, and he promised to raise up all; and when he was present, he gave life to whom he wished, so that what is said is: of the Father in the beginning, of the Son in the working-out, and of the Spirit in the participation, being a partaker of him and as if being brought through the Son into the life of all, according to: 'He will give life to your mortal bodies through the Spirit who dwells in you' (Ps 103:31). The Spirit is indeed life-giving, through which he works life, and God-making, through which he gives participation and the human spirit is of the same name according to its formation by him (Ps 103:32).

Eternal is the glory of him who preserves his works forever; and since the glory is eternal, the things being glorified are eternal (Ps 103:33). The magnitude of the glory is shown by the awe of the creation, and the subjection is signaled by the awe. Thus the psalm says that the sea is made subject by being terrified (Ps 103:34). For what fears, submits; and the subjection of the earth is the trembling of the oversight of God, and the smoking of the mountains, as if they were burning, which was seen bodily on Sinai (Ps 103:33-34). This is the gain of life; for this it is worthy to live; therefore death is terrible, the one silencing the...
The text ends abruptly mid-clause.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Kindness and Severity
english: Death is a loss, because there is no one in death remembering you, and life is merely existence because those living, he says, will praise you. For we have being through connection to the One who is, and separation is corruption. My discourse pleased him, and I shall be glad in the Lord; and he is worthy of prayer, so that God may be glad through our hymns, and we may have joy through them in every way. Even if all this were such that all our actions were a hymn to God, God would be glad for us, just as he was glad from the beginning.

One should not ignore, he says, that he is the Lord our God, whose providence governs the whole universe with divine judgments, so that nothing happens unsuitably or without his providence (Ps 104:7). [The plagues] were applied without distinction to the ranks of the plagues and he does not leave all [of them] out, for I think the power of God and the ever-spoken wonders are shown; and it is necessary that God's power be made known, and not an uninterrupted history of events (Ps 104:15).

He says the frogs did not come simply to the land, but into the houses, and the most prominent of the houses and their innermost parts, so that their onslaught would be unhindered and most violent, with no one, not even the strongest, being able to prevent it (Ps 104:27). It is also paradoxical that the dust and the lice were poured out over the whole earth and stood at the borders, not spreading further, as if the judgment were being carried out only in Egypt. Therefore, the bloodletting of the river also happened to stop at the borders, while in the neighboring regions the flows were such that, according to the Egyptians, the punishment was the removal of the river's prosperity (Ps 104:37).

Regarding the salvation given and the prosperity, he says [of] the power from God which led the Egyptians away, they ask to provide many and costly things for those about to leave the land. And it is great also to be delivered from suffering, while the land suffers most, until one [is safe] (Ps 105:14). When they tested God in a waterless place, being unchangeable and not forgetful, he did not fail them; he gave them...

Not only regarding their petition, but also when they were ascending in the Red Sea, and then He made His power known to them; but when they mocked Moses and Aaron in the camp, the earth suddenly opened and swallowed them up. For it was necessary that the servants should not be despised.

But also, since kindness and severity are both with Him, according to 'Behold then the kindness and severity of God' (Rom 11:22), first the things of kindness were provided to them; but as they were not able through it, following that, He met them with the medicine of the cauterizer.

Regarding Moses, indeed, those concerning Dathan and Abiram mocked, saying, 'Has God spoken to Moses alone? Has He not also to us?' and Korah and his assembly, daring to bring strange fire and sacrifices to God in the land of the sanctuaries. But for those who spoke against Moses, the earth opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the assembly of Abiram; and for Korah and those with him who were about to offer their incense, a flame proceeding from the Tabernacle burned them.

According to justice, the term is of destruction, but according to philanthropy, the remission is of saving. Regarding the remission, the embassy gave space because of the holiness of the one embassying and the providence for the sake of the world, through which the ambassador pleaded, so that the grace of God regarding Israel might not be considered insufficient; and because of the memory of the fathers and the promise to them, which Moses reminded [God] while pleading, for according to their impiety and the foreknowledge of all their evil, they would have been destroyed.

And the dispute concerning the earth is more ancient than the stand of Korah and Dathan, but greater and more impious, contending against the promise of God and not striving for the healing of God; so it is fitting that it is arranged through the cowardice occurring from the aforementioned impiety toward God, just as that [dispute] occurred through small-mindedness, a despairing of the success of the cowardice, just as the small-mindedness because of the separation of Moses was making a despairing of the return of Moses. For not only desires, but also cowardices and small-mindednesses of those owing to God and those owing to men are taken away, the endurance...

title: Allegory of the Exodus and the Sea
english: Obstacles to honor are produced by disobedience to God and by disorder among men, as the fleshly nature mourns the spiritual [nature] and the beauty beside it vanishes through its own pleasure. But the God of discipline leads things through certain ways; the end of discipline is the correction of man toward the right through the leadership of the spirit, and the obedience of the flesh.

For this reason, he placed the provision of pleasures as a teacher, so that the desire of these might be made subject to the intellect according to the will of God, and he led [them] through dangers, training [them] to endure what is otherwise to be fled from through the hope toward God which is fitting for those who think rightly. And since men are more fleshly in the present state, first he relents from justice toward the disobedient and small-souled, but later, toward a return, he punishes.

Since, indeed, not punishing those shrinking from and arguing against the Red Sea, he punishes those who did not dare to follow him toward the promised land. For it was a manifest sign of unbelief. For to have seen so many and such wonders, to dare [to rebel] against all things was not just by the power of salvation.

And indeed, since having punished the Egyptians less, even though they were more impious, in some parts, he punished more severely with the death of the people in the disobedience of all the people of that time regarding the distribution of the land, because through the former justice they were not made wise and they remained to test God even more. Regarding Psalm 105:28, he did not say the cause of idolatry was that which was fornication, leading them into participation in reverence (for this was related to gluttony), but the result condemns it, for the sake of which also the law spoke of the mixing with women of foreign nations, lest they should fall into participation in impiety through the sympathy of the women, which indeed happened. For it led them so far into madness, as to be initiated into the things of Beelzebub and to be joined in sacrifices performed by the dead.

In Psalm 105:46-47, in this he shows that the return of the captives through mercy would not remain unshaken, having brought a prayer concerning the gathering from the nations and ending in this, so that they might find the salvation from God himself to be firm and immovable and through all things give thanks to the Savior and the [life] in God.

They have joy. And it is necessary for mercy to receive those after their present unbelief, as the apostle says, so that having been petitioned, they may dance to God all the days, as Zechariah foretells (Ps 106:6).

He says these things concerning the Jews: first, having been freed from the oppression in Egypt by crying out to the Lord, now, being subject to the same things and being delivered from all kinds of wandering, if they would cry out to the Lord, they might happen to reach the perfect liberty through Christ. And this is the same allegory, whence it does not seem at all that these things are being allegorized. For the words spoken do not suit the idea of the same people wandering in a desert and being bound in a dark prison. But it is clear according to Isaiah, he who says to those in bonds, 'Come forth,' and to those in darkness, 'Be uncovered,' concerning which Zechariah [says] that by His blood His covenant sent the prisoners out of a pit without water. Christ is therefore Savior from the Father, and Father through Christ. But Israel is being covered by death now, and is bound by humility and by the necessity of slavery. For the covering is a shadow, but humility is poverty, and necessity is iron. And for the Gentiles, they establish them being cast into a land of the nations, the poor from the beginning, concerning whom the 105th Psalm says, 'The poor shall eat and be satisfied' (Ps 105:9).

Allegorizing the evils of the Jews as wandering, famine, thirst, darkness, and bonds, he uses now an allegory of mariners: the disturbances in the sea and the transformations from these into prosperity, and leading them even unto a prosperous salvation through these labors; and he who has received the labors shall find rest, not without God having been disturbed into waves their former calm, but they show it by a divine command, just as one having raised a storm by command and having shaken their former prosperous sailing with the waves, by which they are being lifted up to a height and tossed down, as it happens to be in the sea, being humbled and being poured out and being tossed about by an ecstasy; then to experience a change by the wind, whenever God might command this, and He releases the violence of the winds into a gentle breeze and quiets the sound of the waves, where...
